html:
A hilltop castle in Himeji, west of Kobe in Japan, whose main keep was completed in 1609. It is the finest surviving Japanese castle, often called White Heron Castle for its white plaster walls and roofs that seem to spread like wings.

A fort stood on the hill from the 1300s, and Toyotomi Hideyoshi held it in the 1580s. After the battle of Sekigahara in 1600, Tokugawa Ieyasu gave the domain to his son in law Ikeda Terumasa, who rebuilt it on a grand scale. The complex has 83 buildings, with a maze of gates and paths meant to confuse attackers, slits for guns and arrows, and holes for dropping stones.

It was never seriously attacked. It survived the order of the Meiji government to demolish castles, and in 1945 American bombs burned much of the city around it but left it standing. It was among the first Japanese sites named to the World Heritage list, in 1993.
